newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco attorney urges judge to dismiss Texas suit.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco attorney urges judge to dismiss Texas suit.

text.p: Tobacco company attorneys urged a U.S. federal judge on Monday to throw out a $4 billion suit filed by Texas Attorney General Dan Morales to recover taxpayers' money he said was spent treating poor people for smoking-related illnesses.

Morales' suit uses a statistical model to estimate the cost to Texas taxpayers of smoking-related illnesses among poor people who receive federally mandated medical treatment through the Medicaid program.

The suit charges the tobacco companies with violating federal racketeering statutes, federal and state antitrust laws, along with negligence, unjust enrichment, fraud, deceptive acts, breach of express or implied warranties, and violating strict liability laws for abnormally dangerous activity and for defective products.
Philip Morris Cos. Inc. counsel Dan Webb asked U.S. District Court Judge David Folsom to throw out all 14 counts in the suit.

Webb said three counts, based on federal racketeering statutes, were inappropriate because injury to business or property was not allowed for expenses related to personal injury and because the tobacco companies do not constitute a "viable enterprise" that acted in concert.

He also said the state's only appropriate remedy to recoup Medicaid losses was by filing individual claims on behalf of each of the recipients. He said the state was aware of cautionary reports about possible smoking hazards when it chose to license and tax the sale of cigarettes rather than ban them.

But Lawrence Tribe, representing the state, said the overriding issue was that the losses incurred by "innocent, non-smoking taxpayers" were the direct result of "one of the most massive conspiracies in history" against children and adults.
"The payment of taxes is not a license to addict children," he said.

Tribe said the personal injury exclusion cited by the defense did not apply because the state was not trying to obtain financial relief for the individual Medicaid patients but for the state's finances, which were injured because of the cost of medical care for individuals who smoked.

Webb said the statistical model, which was devoid of specific individual cases that could be defended by questioning Medicaid patients about their smoking habits and other lifestyle issues, denied the tobacco companies due process. "This should be addressed on a case-by-case basis."
The courtroom errupted in laughter when U.S. District Court Judge David Folsom asked Webb, "How many generations will that take?"
Webb said: "If you rule for my motion (to dismiss the suit), not many."
Tribe said later that using a statistical model of aggregate losses would keep the case from becoming "a multi-headed hydra" of individual suits or a class action.

The suit, scheduled for trial on Sept. 29, was filed against Philip Morris; R.J. Reynolds Tobacco, a division of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. ; Brown and Williamson Tobacco Corp., which is owned by B.A.T Industries Plc ; Lorillard Tobacco Co; United States Tobacco Co; Hill & Knowlton Inc; the Council for Tobacco Research-USA (successor to Tobacco Institute Research Committee), and the Tobacco Institute Inc.
